candidates.text:
Agni I laud, the divine household-priest of the sacrifice, the seasonal officiant, the Hotṛ, the most generous bestower of treasures.
Agni, lauded by the ancient seers and by those of today — may he convey the gods hither.
Through Agni may one attain wealth and prosperity day by day — wealth glorious and abounding in heroes.
O Agni, whatever unblemished sacrifice you encompass on all sides — that one truly reaches the gods.
May Agni the Hotṛ, of poet-wisdom, true, most rich in varied fame, come hither as a god among the gods.
Whatever good, O Agni, you will bestow upon the worshipper — that is indeed your truth, O Aṅgiras.
To you, O Agni, day by day, at the dusk and at the dawn, we come with prayer bearing homage.
To him who reigns over the sacrifices, the guardian of ṛta who shines bright, who grows mighty in his own house —

O Agni, sacrifice here to the Vasus, the Rudras, and the Ādityas; sacrifice to the people born of Manu, the Manu-born folk who sprinkle ghee, making the rite auspicious.
For the gods, O Agni, are prompt to heed the worshipper, they are discerning; bring them here, O you praised with songs, O you whose horses are red — all thirty-three.
As for Priyamedha, as for Atri, O Jātavedas, as for Virūpa, as for the Aṅgirases — O you of great vows, hear the call of Praskaṇva.
The Priyamedhas called on the great-horned one for aid — Agni, the king of sacrifices, blazing with brilliant splendor.
O you who are invoked with ghee, these words are real and true — hear them; with these songs the sons of Kaṇva call upon you for protection.
You, of most wondrous fame, O Agni, O hair of flame, O most beloved — the beings among the clans call upon you to carry their oblations.

The eager days have come around for you; this thought of the Vārkaras, and the divine song — making the brahman-prayer, the Gotamas with their songs have pushed upward the reservoir to drink from.
This and that has Gotama made known to you by the road, O Maruts — beholding your gold-wheeled, iron-tusked wild boars racing on.
This song of yours, O Maruts, the bearer that accompanies — the voice of the worshipping priest resounds back; it has resounded in the wake of the self-born ones' own nature, from the fist.
May auspicious thoughts come to us from all sides, undeluded, unenclosed, opening up; may the gods ever be for our increase — those who are unaging guardians day by day.
May the gracious will of the gods come to those who are upright; may the gift of the gods turn back toward us. We have attained the friendship of the gods; may the gods extend our life so that we may live.

Before the Sun emerged from the darkness — O stone-wielder — you seized his cleft weapon. Even the might of Śuṣṇa that was set around him, firmly knotted from heaven — that you took away.
The two great expanses, Heaven and Earth, rejoiced following your deed, O Indra — let them exult. You slew with the great thunderbolt Vṛtra lying across the streams, the boar.
O Indra, heroic one — the men you favored, stand with the best-harnessed team of the wind. The exhilarating, Vṛtra-slaying thunderbolt for crossing over which the wise Uśanā Kāvya gave you — he fashioned it.
For this his might the seers, the Ṛbhus of good insight, fashioned their hymns and songs — those who illumine the glories of the prize-winning, the sacrificial — and Sarasvatī, the light of the Sun.
And indeed gazing at that one's act — the fathers at the sacrifice looked below like those of the lower one. I praise Ṛbhu and Cakra for their insight; may all beings cross over for his sake.

The seven who stand on this seven-wheeled chariot — seven horses draw it. Seven sisters call out together, where the seven names of the cattle are set down.
Who saw the one being born first, the one with bones, which the boneless one bears? The earth's vital breath, blood, and soul — where are they? Who has gone to the wise one to ask this?
Childlike I ask, not knowing in my mind — what are the hidden tracks of the gods there? The poets have stretched out, as if for weaving, seven threads upon the young calf — so they say.
Not knowing, even among the knowing, I ask the poet-seers here for the sake of knowledge, I who do not know — what is the one thing that in the form of the unborn has propped up these six spaces apart?
Let him speak here who truly knows the hidden track of this lovely bird. The cows milk milk from his head; clothed in wrappings they have drunk water with their feet.

Growing great on the pressed, exhilarating drink of Trita, he has struck down the myriad serpents. Indra with the Aṅgirases has turned the sun like a wheel; he has cloven Vala.
Now may that bountiful right hand of yours, O Indra, yield to your singer the choicest gift. Grant aid to the praisers; let our share not be consumed. May we speak great words at the assembly, possessed of heroes.
He who, as soon as born, was the first thinker, the god who encompassed the gods with his power of will — from whose might the two world-halves trembled in fear at the greatness of his manly force — he, O people, is Indra.
He who made firm the trembling earth; he who stilled the mountains when they were enraged; he who measured out the atmosphere more widely; he who propped up the sky — he, O people, is Indra.

O Vaiśvānara, I delight in your abodes by which you became the discerning finder of light. Being born, you filled all worlds and both spheres; O Agni, you are all-encompassing of yourself.
The seer alone has emitted a great stream from the wondrous powers of Vaiśvānara through his own artistry. Agni was born magnifying both parents, heaven and earth, rich in seed.
Fuel-stave by fuel-stave, be kindly wakeful for us; flame by flame, bestow favour along with wealth. O god, bring the gods here for the sacrifice; as their friend you shall worship your friends with a good mind, O Agni.
The one whom the gods — Varuṇa, Mitra, Agni — honour three times on each day: make this sweet sacrifice of ours, which Tanūnapāt and Ghee-womb have distributed, a success.
The all-chosen sacred thought goes forth to honour the Hotṛ as the first for worship. To approach the bull with homages and praise him — so summoned and most sacrificing, let him worship the gods.

Let the sacred prayer penetrate thy two flanks, O Indra, and thy head; and reach thy two arms, O hero, for the bestowal of bounty.
The offering with parched grain, the mixture with groats, the cake, together with the laud — be pleased with these of ours at dawn, O Indra.
The cake to be cooked, O Indra — be pleased with it and accept it; for thee the oblations are poured out.
Enjoy our sacrificial cake and delight in our hymns, as a bridegroom delights in maidens.
The sacrificial cake at the morning pressing — be pleased with ours, O thou who hast been praised of old; for thy will, O Indra, is great.
Make the parched grains and the sacrificial cake of the midday pressing beautiful here, O Indra; when the praiser, the singer, swift of purpose, desiring thee, approaches thee with hymns.

What excellent praise has turned the son of might — Indra — hither toward bounty? The hero gives goods to the one who praises him; he is the lord of the herd — let him, O people, drive away our obstacles.
He is to be called upon at the slaying of Vṛtra; he is to be praised — the truly bountiful Indra, well-lauded. He who, on his course, O Maghavan, for the mortal who prays and presses well, establishes broad space.
Him men call forth variously in battle — those who have left behind their bodies making a shield. When both parties have met the mutual abandonment — men in the winning of offspring and progeny.
The peoples exert their wills in the fierce yoking — eager for mutual flood-winning. When the warrior clans turn against each other in battle, then these ones make Indra their concern in the encounter.

In the praise of this generous one, the friend of the one whose flame has grown — in him in the greatly resounding battle they have placed all vigor.
Thus truly, O Agni, by the generosity of their good heroic power — around him, great as the two world-halves, fame has come to be.
Come now, praised, O Agni, and bring the desirable thing; we who along with the lords set forth well-being together — and be present for our growth in battles.
With sacrifices, O god, the mortal in this way, for the aid of the mightier — Pūru would invoke Agni at the good rite, with the deed done, for protection.
For of this one you think more self-gloriously in the mouth by virtue of his dispensation; him the exhilarating one of variegated flame, surpassing by his vision.
Clothed in this one's flame is he who is harnessed with swift song; his flames blaze greatly like the seed of heaven.

Those who carry this with their swift horses, drinking the intoxicating sweet drink — here they have established their glories.
By whose splendour the two worlds gleam as if in their chariots — like gold above in the sky.
Young is this Marut host, of impetuous chariots, unsurpassed, going beauteously, unopposed.
Who now knows where these spotless ones, born from the cosmic order, are exhilarated as they shake?
You, O praiseworthy ones, are the leaders of mortal man, guiding him with your thought, the hearers at the callings for your help.
May those destroyers of foes, adorable, of manifold brilliance, turn to us with desirable riches.
O divine Ūrmī, carry this my hymn forth to Dārbhya, like a charioteer (carries) praises.
And let them say to me thus in the presence of Rathavīti who has pressed the soma: 'My desire does not go away from me.'

Him I praise — Indra, who is knowing, who is carried by praises, who grows through sacrifice with hymns; whose greatness, full of many forms, surpasses that of heaven and earth.
He spread out the darkness, the formless void, and made it luminous with the sun; when do mortals, seeking the station of the immortal, not injure it, self-sustaining as they are?
Where is that Indra who made these things? Among what people does he move? In which tribes? What sacrifice of yours is pleasing to his mind for choosing? What song of praise, O Indra? Which is he, the ritual priest?
Even those ancient ones born before thee, who acted much — your friends — they gladdened you with praises; those who are of the middle age, and those of recent times, and those of the very latest — be mindful of them, O much-invoked Indra.

Purupanthā has given for the hymn to you two Nāsatyas a hundred of the thousand-horsed; now, O hero, has given for the hymn to Bharadvāja; may you, of many wonders, lay the demons low.
May we be in your favour, in your breadth, O Aśvins, with the patrons.
The splendours of the glowing dawn have risen up like the shining waves of the waters; she makes all roads easy, all paths good; the bounteous sacrificial fee has become rich and reward-bestowing.
Auspicious to behold, you shine forth widely; your flames and rays have leapt up to the sky; you reveal your breast, adorning yourself, O goddess Uṣas, shining with your might.
The red, shining cows carry her onward, the fortunate one spreading widely; the hero drives away the enemies like arrows; swift darkness presses back like a carrier.

He, the discerner, knowing both worlds, giver of thousands and one who possesses eternally — Vasiṣṭha was born amid the Apsarases, about to weave the enclosure stretched by Yama.
Born together at the sacrifice, urged by devotion, they poured their commingled seed into a jar; thence Māna rose up in the midst; thence the seer born is called Vasiṣṭha.
He bears the bearer of laud, the bearer of Sāman, and bearing the pressing-stone he speaks forth first; approach him with goodwill — Vasiṣṭha will come to you, O Pratṛdas.
Let the divine bright prayer go forth from us, well-fashioned as a swift racing-chariot.
The flowing waters hear and know the birth-place of earth and heaven.
Even the wide waters swell for him; in the battles against Vṛtras the mighty champions take thought.

The wise and radiant one, who increases wealth and whose lustre clings to rich food, accompanies the swift teams. For Vāyu's sake those men of one accord spread abroad, and performed all things for the welfare of their offspring.
So far as the vigour of the body, so far as the strength, so far as the men contemplating with vision — O pure drinkers Indra-Vāyu, drink the pure Soma pressed for us; be seated on this sacred grass.
Harnessing your desirable steeds, the swift teams, O Indra-Vāyu, come hither on one chariot. For this is the first portion of the mead offered to you; be satisfied and release your bounty upon us.
Whatever hundred, whatever thousand swift teams belonging to you, O Indra-Vāyu, all-desirable, attend you — with these most excellent ones come hither, O heroes, and drink of the mead that is offered.

The leader forward to better things, the maker of light in battles — the ever-victorious one who has conquered enemies in battle.
He the protector shall carry us across in safety — the much-invoked Indra — beyond all enemies.
So thou, O Indra, with prizes and with favour and with a good path — lead thou us to grace.
Come hither, for this soma is delicious to thee; O Indra, drink this; here is the sacred grass, my seat for thee.
Let the two maned bay steeds yoked by prayer carry thee, O Indra; hear our prayers.
We the prayer-bearers with our ally invoke thee, O Indra the soma-drinker, we who possess soma, we who press the soma.
Come to us who press soma, to our excellent praises; drink well of the soma-juice, O thou of mighty jaws.
I pour into thy two flanks; let it flow through the limbs; take the honey with thy tongue.

Being kindled here, O brilliant-flaming, truthful one, bring hither, discerning, the divine company.
The inspired Hotṛ, unbeguiling, with banner of smoke, luminously wealthy — the banner of sacrifices we implore.
O Agni, protect us; O god, ward off those who would harm us; shatter enmity, O mighty one.
Agni, adorning his own body with ancient meditation, the seer has increased with the inspired hymn.
I call hither the son of strength, Agni of purifying flame, to this sacrificial rite, this good sacrifice.
O Agni, great as Mitra, with your brilliant flame, take your seat on the sacred grass with the gods.
To that mortal who honours Agni, the god, at home in his own body — to him may he shine forth wealth.
Agni is the head, the peak of heaven; lord of the earth is he; he quickens the seeds of the waters.

Step forward boldly, O bold one, and bring to us the treasure of him who has not pressed soma — him who is the more unworthy.
O Indra, whatever prize of yours is to be won through inspired poets — do win it well for us.
Your prizes, swift as the speed of a day, all-glittering, and the willing steeds — may they come quickly at our desire.
Run forward here, O Vṛtra-slayer, from far away and from near, to the pouring out of the sweet drink.
Come hither: the soma juices are strong and pressed, intoxicating; drink steadily as is your wont.
Exhilarate yourself with food; indeed it is fit for your desire and your mood; may it be good for your heart, O Indra.
Come, O you who have no foe, come hither; you are also invoked for the recitations in the highest luminous realm of heaven.

This indeed is that bull-like chariot which streams with the sheep's-wool strands, going to win the thousandfold prize.
The maidens of Trita urge this tawny one forward with the pressing-stones — the Indu for Indra to drink.
The ten tawny mares, eager for action, cleanse him — those by whom he shines for the exhilaration.
This one settles among human settlements like a falcon, going like a lover toward a woman.
This intoxicating juice, the child of heaven, gazes down, this Indu who has entered the woolen filter.
This pressed tawny one, the steady one, streams for drinking, calling out toward his dear birthplace.
Flow swiftly, O Soma, for him of great wisdom, around with your dear abode — where the gods declare you to be.
Adorning what is unadorned, dispensing refreshments to the people, flow around as the rain of heaven.

He stirs up blessings, those rich in progeny, all life-giving, all well-nourishing day by day; O Indu, when drunk, may you ask Indra to grant us sacred prayer with offspring, riches, and a household of horses.
He, the tawny, desirable exhilaration, first among the days, makes himself known with his mind day by day; moving between two peoples, he goes along — both that of men and the divine ordainer.
They anoint him, they anoint him separately, they anoint him together; they lick his will with honey, they anoint him; in the swelling of the river, the golden-purifying ones seize the flying bull among the waters.
Sing to the wise Pavamāna; his mighty stream flows, the plant-extract rushes; like a serpent creeping over a parched skin, the tawny bull has rushed along playing like a swift horse.

Hear us, O Agni, in the assembly, in the gathering-place; yoke thy chariot swift as the immortal. Bring hither to us Heaven and Earth, divine children; may thou never depart from the gods' company here.
I yoke you two with the ancient sacred word, with reverences; may the hymn go forth like the sage's [chant] along its path. May all the sons of the immortal hear, even those who have taken up their stations in the divine realms.
When you two came forth as the two striving [like a pair of twins], men devoted to the gods brought oblations to you. Take your own place, you who know it well — be a good seat for Indu [Soma] among us.
I have mounted the five-footed [gāyatrī]; I follow the four-footed [triṣṭubh] according to sacred law. By the syllable I measure this [speech]; at the navel of Order [ṛta] I purify it together.

I, Indra, having raised the obstruction and nurtured the Atharvan, produced the cows upon the serpent for Trita. I seize the manly power away from the Dasyus; teaching the cow-pen, [I give] to Dadhīca and Mātariśvan.
For me Tvaṣṭṛ fashioned the iron bolt; in me the gods have bent their will. My face is hard to endure like that of the sun; people approach me with what has been done and what is to be done.
I sharpen this cattle-winning, horse-winning animal — the one rich in food, golden, with an arrow-swift [movement] — many thousands [I give] to the worshipper, when the soma-draughts with their lauds have gladdened me.
I, Indra, have never lost the prize; I have never yielded to death at any time. Press soma and ask me for riches; O Pūrus, do not fall into ruin in my friendship.

May Pūṣan lead you from here, taking you by the hand; may the Aśvins carry you onward in their chariot. Go to your home so that you may be mistress of the house; speak your will in the assembly.
Here may your dear happiness with offspring be fulfilled; be wakeful in this house for the gṛhapati fire. Unite your body with your husband; thus growing old together you shall speak in the assembly.
Dark-red it becomes; the spell attached to the garment is expelled. Her kinsmen prosper; the husband is bound in bonds.
Give away the garment of ill omen; distribute the wealth to the Brāhmaṇas. Let this witchcraft go on its way; may the wife enter her husband as the good one.
The body becomes inauspicious, glittering and dangerous, when the husband covers his own limb with the bride's garment.

Fourteen are the greatnesses of this one; the seven wise ones guide him with speech. Who here would declare the far-reaching ford, by which path they drink up the pressed soma?
The fifteen praises in a thousandfold — as far as Heaven and Earth extend, so far is that. Thousandfold the greatnesses, a thousand — as far as brahman is spread, so great is speech.
What wise one knows the yoking of the metres? Who has attained the word directed to the bright one? Who, they say, is the eighth heroic priest? Who really has discerned the two tawny horses of Indra?
Some roam about the ends of the earth; they stand on the shafts of the chariot, yoked. Among these they distribute the share of fatigue when Yama is placed in the dwelling.
Wondrous indeed is the growth of this young child who does not go to his two mothers to suckle. If he was born uncollected, yet straightway he grew; running his great messenger's course at once.

In raptures we admire thy bold design,
And, as the subject, own the hand divine.
While thro' thy work the rising day shall stream,
So long shall last thy honour, praise, and name.
And may thy labours to the Muse impart
Some emanation from her sister art,
To animate the verse, and bid it shine
In colours easy, bright, and strong, as Thine.
Supine on earth an awful figure lies,
While softest slumbers seem to seal his eyes;
The hoary sire Heaven's guardian care demands,
And at his feet the watchful angel stands.
The form august and large, the mien divine
Betray the founder of Messiah's line.
Lo! from his loins the promis'd stem ascends,
And high to Heaven its sacred Boughs extends:

Could the warm sun, as erst when Memnon play'd,
Wake with his rising beam the vocal shade:
Then might he draw th' attentive angels down,
Bending to hear the lay, so sweet, so like their own.
On either side the monarch's offspring shine,
And some adorn, and some disgrace their line.
Here Ammon glories; proud, incestuous lord!
This hand sustains the robe, and that the sword.
Frowning and fierce, with haughty strides he towers,
And on his horrid brow defiance low'rs.
There Absalom the ravish'd sceptre sways,
And his stol'n honour all his shame displays:
The base usurper Youth! who joins in one
The rebel subject, and th' ungrateful son.
Amid the royal race, see Nathan stand:
Fervent he seems to speak, and lift his hand;

Fix'd Contemplation hold his steady eyes —
I know the Sage; the wisest of the wise.
Blest with all man could wish, or prince obtain,
Yet his great heart pronounc'd those blessings vain.
And lo! bright glittering in his sacred hands,
In miniature the glorious temple stands.
Effulgent frame! stupendous to behold!
Gold the strong valves, the roof of burnish'd gold.
The wandering ark, in that bright dome inshrin'd,
Spreads the strong light, eternal, unconfin'd!
Above th' unutterable glory plays
Presence divine! and the full-streaming rays
Pour thro' reluctant crowds intolerable blaze.
But stern Oppression rends Reboam's reign;
See the gay prince, injurious, proud, and vain!
Th' imperial sceptre totters in his hand,

He, the just prince — with every virtue blest,
He reign'd, and goodness all the man possest,
Around his throne, fair happiness and peace
Smooth'd every brow, and smil'd in every face.
As when along the burning waste he stray'd,
Where no pure streams in bubbling mazes play'd,
Where drought incumbent on the thirsty ground,
Long since had breath'd her scorching blasts around;
The prophet calls, th' obedient floods repair
To the parch'd fields, for Josaphat was there.
The new-sprung waves, in many a gurgling vein,
Trickle luxurious thro' the sucking plain;
Fresh honours the reviving fields adorn,
And o'er the desart Plenty pours her horn.
So, from the throne his influence he sheds,
And bids the Virtues raise their languid heads:

Transmissive worth adorns the pious Son,
The father's virtues with the father's throne.
Lo! there he stands: he who the rage subdued
Of Ammon's sons, and drench'd his sword in blood,
And dost thou, Ahaz, Judah's scourge, disgrace,
With thy base front, the glories of thy race?
See the vile King his iron sceptre bear —
His only praise attends the pious Heir;
He, in whose soul the virtues all conspire,
The best good son, from the most wicked sire.
And lo! in Hezekiah's golden reign,
Long-exil'd Piety returns again;
Again, in genuine purity she shines,
And with her presence gilds the long-neglected shrines.
Ill-starr'd does proud Assyria's impious Lord
Bid Heaven to arms, and vaunt his dreadful sword;

And rolls full fifteen summers o'er thy head;
Lo! the receding sun repeats his way,
And, like thy life, prolongs the falling day.
Tho' Nature her inverted course forego,
The day forget to rest, the time to flow,
Yet shall Jehovah's servants stand secure,
His mercy fix'd, eternal shall endure;
On them her ever-healing rays shall shine;
More mild, and bright, and sure, O sun! than thine.
At length, the long-expected Prince behold,
The last good King; in ancient days foretold,
When Bethel's altar spoke his future fame,
Rent to its base, at good Josiah's name.
Blest, happy prince! o'er whose lamented urn,
In plaintive song, all Judah's daughters mourn;
For whom sad Sion's softest Sorrow flows,

And Jeremiah pours his sweet melodious woes.
But now fall'n Sion, once the fair and great,
Sits deep in dust, abandon'd, desolate;
Bleeds her sad heart, and ever stream her eyes,
And anguish tears her, with convulsive sighs.
The mournful captive spreads her hands in vain,
Her hands, that rankle with the servile chain;
Till he, Great Chief! in Heaven's appointed time.
Leads back her children to their native clime.
Fair Liberty revives with all her joys,
And bids her envy'd walls securely rise.
And thou, great hallow'd dome, in ruin spread,
Again shall lift sublime thy sacred head.
But ah! with weeping eyes, the ancients view
A faint resemblance of the old in you.
No more th' effulgent glory of thy God

But now alas! far other views disclose
The blackest comprehensive scene of woes.
See where man's voluntary sacrifice
Bows his meek head, and God Eternal dies!
Fixt to the Cross, his healing arms are bound,
While copious Mercy streams from every wound.
Mark the blood-drops that life exhausting roll,
And the strong pang that rends the stubborn soul!
As all death's tortures, with severe delay,
Exult and riot in the noblest prey,
And can'st thou, stupid man, those sorrows see,
Nor share the anguish which He bears for Thee?
Thy sin, for which his sacred Flesh is torn,
Points every nail, and sharpens every thorn;
Canst thou? — while Nature smarts in every wound,
And each pang cleaves the sympathetic ground!

The molten doluge round the globe shall roar,
And all man's arts and labour be no more.
Then shall the splendors of th' enliven'd glass
Sink undistinguish'd in the burning mass.
And O! till earth, and seas, and Heaven decay,
Ne'er may that fair creation fade away;
May winds and storms those beauteous colours spare,
Still may they bloom, as permanent as fair,
All the vain rage of wasting time repell,
And his Tribunal see, whose Cross they paint so well.
The CHOICE of HERCULES.
A POEM.
NOW had the son of Jove mature, attain'd
The joyful prime: when youth, elate and gay,
Steps into life; and follows unrestrain'd
Where passion leads, or prudence points the way.

"Mature the copious harvest shall be thine;
"Let the laborious hind subdue the soil:
"Leave the rash soldier spoils of war to win;
"Won by the soldier thou shalt share the spoil:
"These softer cares my blest allies employ,
"New pleasures to invent; to wish, and to enjoy. "
Her winning voice the youth attentive caught:
He gaz'd impatient on the smiling maid;
Still gaz'd, and listen'd: then her name besought:
"My name, fair youth, is Happiness, she said.
"Well can my friends this envy'd truth maintain:
"They share my bliss; they best can speak my praise:
"Tho' slander call me Sloth — detraction vain!
"Heed not what Slander, vain detractor, says:
"Slander, still prompt true merit to defame;
"To blot the brightest worth, and blast the fairest name."

By this, arriv'd the fair majestic maid:
(She all the while, with the same modest pace,
Compos'd, advanc'd.) "Know, Hercules," she said
With manly tone, "thy birth of heav'nly race;
"Thy tender age that lov'd instruction's voice,
"Promis'd thee generous, patient, brave and wise;
"When manhood should confirm thy glorious choice:
"Now expectation waits to see thee rise.
"Rise, youth! Exalt thyself, and me: approve
"Thy high descent from heav'n; and dare be worthy Jove.
"But what truth prompts, my tongue shall not disguise;
"The steep ascent must be with toil subdu'd:
"Watching and cares must win the lofty prize
"Propos'd by heav'n; true bliss, and real good.
"Honour rewards the brave and bold alone;
"She spurns the timorous, indolent, and base:

"First conquer thou thyself. To ease, to rest,
"To each soft thought of pleasure, bid farewel.
"The night alternate, due to sweet repose,
"In watches waste; in painful march, the day:
"Congeal'd, amidst the rigorous winter's snows;
"Scorch'd, by the summer's thirst-inflaming ray.
"Thy harden'd limbs shall boast superior might:
"Vigour shall brace thine arm, resistless in the fight. "
"Hear'st thou, what monsters then thou must engage;
"What dangers, gentle youth, she bids thee prove?
(Abrupt says Sloth) "ill fit thy tender age
"Tumult and wars; fit age, for joy and love.
"Turn, gentle youth, to me, to love and joy!
"To these I lead: no monsters here shall stay
"Thine easy course; no cares thy peace annoy:
"I lead to bliss a nearer, smoother way.

"For thou art only tir'd with indolence:
"Nor is thy sleep, with toil and labour bought:
"Th' imperfect sleep that lulls thy languid sense
"In dull oblivious interval of thought:
"That kindly steals th' inactive hours away
"From the long, ling'ring space, that lengthens out the day.
"From bounteous nature's unexhausted stores
"Flows the pure fountain of sincere delights:
"Averse to her, you waste the joyless hours;
"Sleep drowns thy days, and riot rules thy nights.
